field.label: Sequence
field.help: When two classes match one connection, the lower number sets its DSCP.

field.label: Description
field.help: A name for the class, shown after "Traffic Priority:" in OPNsense's rules file, /tmp/rules.debug. It cannot end with a backslash.

field.label: Interfaces
field.help: Where connections come in. None chosen: every interface. Connections a port forward (Firewall: NAT: Destination NAT) lets in with its Firewall rule set to Pass are not marked: pf passes them without reading any filter rule. Set it to Register rule, or to Manual with a rule of your own.

field.label: IP version
field.help: IPv4 by default. On an XGS appliance with os-xgs-npu, a marked IPv6 connection stays with the host - its fast path does not write an IPv6 traffic class - so that connection is not forwarded in hardware.

field.label: Protocol
field.help: A port needs TCP, UDP or TCP/UDP.

field.label: Source
field.help: Where connections come from: an address or a network, aliases, interface networks. any: every source.

field.label: Groups and users
field.help: Groups and users of User Identity (os-useridentity): the connections that come from the addresses it maps to them now - their devices - are this class's, by User Identity's tables. They take the place of Source, which stays any. A connection keeps the mark it opened with: one a device opened before its address was mapped is not marked, the ones after it are - and where os-xgs-npu's cut list holds User Identity's tables, such a connection is cut when the address is mapped, and opens again marked. A group or a user with no table now - User Identity off, the row switched off, or not applied there yet - adds nothing; while none of them has one, the class makes no rule at all, and the Applied tab says why.

field.label: Source port
field.help: Port connections come from, mostly left empty: a number, a name, a range (10000-20000) or an alias of ports.

field.label: Destination
field.help: Where connections go: an address or a network, aliases, interface networks or (self), the firewall itself. any: every destination.

field.label: Applications
field.help: Applications Application Control (os-appcontrol) keeps a table for - those chosen there in Application tables, Blocked applications or Rules, and applied: the connections to the servers nDPI named as one of them are this class's. They take the place of Destination, which stays any. nDPI names a connection 10 to 70 seconds after it begins, so the connection that brings a server into the table is not marked; those opened to it after are, while the server stays in the table (Application Control's Expire, an hour by default). A server two applications share is in both tables. And a device names its own connections: one that writes an application's name to a server of its own has its connections to that server marked too - a class without a minimum can then take a whole port, so give such a class a minimum, or narrow it by Groups and users or Source. While none of them has a table, the class makes no rule at all.

field.label: Application categories
field.help: Categories of nDPI's, each a table Application Control (os-appcontrol) keeps of the servers of every application it named in the category - one for every category, while it classifies. Beside Applications, a connection to either is this class's. What Applications says of when a connection is marked, of servers shared, and of names a device writes itself, holds here too.

field.label: Destination port
field.help: Port connections go to: a number, a name (sip, https), a range (10000-20000) or an alias of ports.

field.label: Arriving with DSCP
field.help: Only connections whose first packet arrives with this DSCP - a phone or a game that marks its own traffic, say. Any: whatever they carry. Best Effort (0) cannot be told apart from Any in pf.

field.label: Set DSCP
field.help: DSCP pf writes into every packet of this class's connections, both ways, their two ECN bits left as they came. EF (46) is the usual mark for voice. A mark is fixed when a connection opens: a change reaches new connections. Firewall: Shaper probably sees the mark on uploads only, not measured: pf writes it as a packet comes in on the class's interface, and on a reply as it leaves by it, so a download arriving on the WAN still carries the DSCP it came with.

field.label: Minimum
field.help: On an XGS 3300 whose switch os-xgs-npu sets: the part of a full port, in percent, this class's switch queue gets at least. Without minimums the classes in the switch are strict, served before everything else, and can take a whole port; with them their queues are weighted and the rest of the port keeps what is left. To keep the parts, os-xgs-npu turns off flow control (pause) on the coprocessor's uplink while the switch has them, and puts it back as it found it when it has none: the switch then drops what the coprocessor sends beyond what a port takes, instead of holding the coprocessor back. Measured on an XGS 3300: minimums of 30 and 20 shared a full port 59 to 41, where with the pause on the first took 98 percent; it cost 1 to 4 percent of the port's rate, and more retransmissions. Strict classes leave the pause as it was. Strict and weighted are not mixed: every class with a switch queue has a minimum, or none has. Only the first two DSCPs in the list's order have a queue of their own, and the minimums of the classes switched on add up to 100 at most. The switch has one set of weights for every port in weighted mode, the coprocessor's own uplink among them, so the part is the same on each; queues 1 to 6, which no class takes, get one turn each in it - frames your clients mark themselves (DSCP 8 to 55) wait in those queues on their way into the coprocessor, and when that link is full each queue gets about one turn in a hundred. Not measured yet: whether the switch shares a port by frames or by bytes.
